I volunteer every Saturday at an animal shelter, and I love it. But I strongly oppose making community service compulsory.

Volunteering means choosing to give your time. When it becomes a requirement, students will do the minimum, watch the clock and treat it as another box to tick. Organisations would have to supervise unwilling teenagers, which takes staff away from real work.

Many students already help their communities in ways that are not counted: caring for younger siblings, working in family shops or looking after sick grandparents. Adding forty hours to their workload, especially in exam years, is unfair.

Encourage volunteering, celebrate it, make it easy to find opportunities. But do not force it.

Our proposed shopping mall on the edge of town will bring more than one hundred shops, a cinema, restaurants and a children's play area under one roof.

Traffic is another concern. Hundreds of cars on narrow rural roads will bring noise, pollution and danger to villages along the route. Heavy rain already floods these fields; building over them could push water into nearby homes.

We support development, but it should use empty buildings and land already built on, not destroy the farms that feed us.

Our weekly market uses tens of thousands of thin plastic bags every day. Most are used for a few minutes and then thrown away. They block drains, causing flooding in the monsoon, and they are eaten by cattle and goats that wander the streets.

We recommend banning thin plastic bags in the market from next year. Cloth and jute bags are cheap, strong and can be reused hundreds of times. Other cities that introduced similar bans have seen cleaner streets and fewer blocked drains within months.

I sell vegetables in the market six days a week. My customers expect a bag, and if I don't give one, they buy from the next stall.

Paper bags tear when tomatoes are wet, and cloth bags cost me far more than plastic. If I have to provide them, my small profit disappears. If I ask customers to pay, they complain.

When bans have been tried before, plastic bags were still sold secretly, and the shopkeepers who obeyed the rules lost out. The real problem is the lack of bins and rubbish collection. Clean the drains, provide bins, and the bags will not end up in the streets.

I am not against protecting the environment. But please do not make the poorest traders pay for it.

Text A: No smartphone before fourteen (a parents' campaign leaflet)

More and more parents are agreeing to wait until their children are at least fourteen before giving them a smartphone.

Young children are not ready for the internet in their pocket. Smartphones expose them to harmful content, contact with strangers and endless games and videos designed to keep them hooked. Sleep, homework and outdoor play suffer.

Children can still have a simple phone for calls and texts, so parents can stay in touch. If enough families agree to wait together, no child need feel left out.

Childhood is short. Let children enjoy it before they enter the online world.

Text B: Banning isn't parenting (a parent's blog)

I understand the worries about smartphones, but I disagree with banning them until fourteen.

My daughter got her first smartphone at eleven. We agreed rules together: no phone at meals or after nine, parental controls, and she tells me if anything online upsets her. She uses it to video-call her grandparents abroad, practise languages and coordinate with friends.

Children who never use smartphones until fourteen suddenly receive one without any experience or guidance, which may be more dangerous. And in many classes, important information is shared in group chats; a child without a phone can genuinely miss out.

Rather than banning, we should be teaching children to use technology safely while we are still there to guide them.

Every morning, the streets outside our schools turn into car parks. Parents double-park, reverse onto pavements and leave engines running, while children squeeze between bumpers.

Text: The potter's wheel

(1) My grandfather's workshop in Multan was a low room at the back of the house, and it smelt permanently of wet earth. Shelves sagged under rows of unglazed pots, and a fine grey dust had settled on everything, including Grandfather himself, who claimed he had not been completely clean for forty years.

(2) For years I had watched him work without daring to ask for a turn. His hands moved with a kind of lazy certainty, coaxing a shapeless lump into a bowl while he talked about cricket or complained about the price of firewood. He never seemed to look at the clay. It simply obeyed him.

(3) The summer I turned fourteen, he pointed at the stool and grunted. I sat down, heart thudding, and he dropped a lump of clay onto the wheel with a wet slap. "Centre it," he said, and folded his arms.

(4) It was like trying to hold down a living animal. The clay lurched and wobbled under my palms, climbing up one side and collapsing on the other. Water ran down my wrists and spattered my shirt. Every time I thought I had tamed it, it bucked away again, and a lopsided tower of mud rose, leaned, and finally sprawled across the wheel like a sleepy dog. Grandfather said nothing. I could feel him not laughing.

(5) It took eleven days before I made anything that could honestly be called a bowl. It was thick-walled, slightly crooked and far too heavy. Grandfather turned it over in his hands for a long time, then placed it on the highest shelf, among his own work. It is still there.

Text: Lost in the market

(1) My parents had warned me to stay close, and for the first hour I did. We drifted through the old market in Marrakesh behind my father's straw hat, past pyramids of spices and stalls hung with brass lamps, while my mother haggled cheerfully over a leather bag she did not need.

(2) Then I stopped to watch a man pouring mint tea from a great height into a row of tiny glasses, and when I looked up the straw hat had vanished. At first I was merely annoyed. I pushed forward to the next corner, certain that I would see them waiting. I did not.

(3) The lanes seemed to multiply around me. Each one was narrower and dimmer than the last, roofed with slatted reeds that sliced the sunlight into thin gold stripes. Donkeys laden with crates squeezed past, forcing me against the walls. Shopkeepers called out to me in three languages, and every voice seemed to be asking where my parents were. The smell of cumin, which had seemed so exciting an hour earlier, now felt suffocating.

(4) I turned left, then right, then left again, and found myself back beside the same carpet stall, its owner watching me with a faint, knowing smile. My throat tightened. I had the absurd thought that the market was deliberately rearranging itself to keep me in.

(5) In the end it was the tea seller who rescued me. He had seen the whole thing, he said, and had sent his nephew running to find a tall foreigner in a straw hat. When my father appeared at the end of the lane, red-faced and breathless, I pretended I had not been worried at all. Nobody believed me.

Text: The old bridge

(1) The bridge had been built by the villagers themselves, long before the road came, and it looked it. Two rusty steel cables were slung across the river, and between them hung a walkway of planks lashed together with wire. Many planks were missing. The gaps were wide enough for a foot, or a child.

(2) My cousin Nadia crossed it every day to reach her school, and she skipped across it now as casually as if it were a pavement, turning halfway to wave at me. The whole structure swayed with her steps, a lazy swing that seemed to go on long after she had reached the far side.

(3) I put one foot on the first plank and felt it shift. Below, the river was the colour of milky tea, swollen with meltwater from the glaciers, and it did not flow so much as hurl itself downstream, roaring and hissing over boulders the size of cars. The noise filled my head. I could not have heard Nadia even if she had shouted.

(4) I edged forward, gripping the cable so hard that the rust bit into my palms. Halfway across, a gust of wind came funnelling down the valley and the bridge lurched beneath me like a startled horse. I froze. For a long moment I was aware of nothing but the gaps between the planks and the brown water churning beneath them.

(5) When I finally stepped onto solid rock, my legs were trembling so badly that I had to sit down. Nadia handed me an apricot from her pocket and said, kindly, that it was much easier the second time. I have never found out whether she was right.

(1) The lift in my aunt's building in Karachi was older than I was, and it behaved like it. It shuddered when the doors closed and groaned between floors, and a handwritten sign inside warned residents, in two languages, not to jump.

(2) I was alone in it, carrying two bags of groceries to the ninth floor, when the lights flickered and died. The lift jolted to a halt with a sound like a dropped cupboard. For a second there was complete darkness. Then a feeble emergency bulb blinked on above my head, casting a dirty orange glow over the scratched steel walls.

(3) Load-shedding, I told myself. The generator would start in a minute. I pressed the alarm button and heard nothing. I pressed it again, harder, as though force might help. Somewhere far below, a dog was barking, and the sound drifted up the shaft, thin and distant, as if from another world.

(4) Minutes passed. The air grew thick and warm, and sweat crept down my back. The walls, which had never seemed close before, now pressed in from every side. I became horribly aware of the shopping at my feet: the eggs, the mangoes, the bottle of milk slowly warming. These ordinary things seemed to belong to a life I had been cut off from.

(5) After twenty-two minutes the generator coughed into life and the lift resumed its journey as if nothing had happened. The doors opened on the ninth floor, and there was my aunt, holding out a glass of cold water. She had been standing there, she said, the whole time.

Text: Arrivals

(1) My grandmother had not been home for nineteen years. She had gone to Manchester to help my uncle when his children were small, and somehow the visit had stretched, year after year, until it became a life. Now she was coming back for good, and the whole family had gathered at the airport to meet her.

(2) The arrivals hall was a battlefield of welcome. Families jostled at the barrier with garlands of roses and marigolds, children rode on shoulders, and someone had brought a drum. Every time the sliding doors parted, the crowd surged forward, scanned the faces, and sank back, disappointed.

A small woman in a grey cardigan was pushing a trolley through the doors, peering anxiously over her glasses at the sea of strangers. (4) Then she saw my father. Her hand flew to her mouth. She left the trolley in the middle of the doorway, to the obvious irritation of a man behind her, and hurried towards the barrier with her arms already open. My father, who never ran anywhere, ran. They met at the end of the rope and held each other, rocking slightly, while the drum thundered and strangers applauded.

(5) In the car she held my hand on her lap the whole way home, as if checking that I was real. She said the mountains looked smaller than she remembered. My father said she had forgotten how tall they were. She said she had forgotten nothing.

Text: The cattle fair

(1) The fair arrived every February, and for a week our dusty town doubled in size. Herders walked in from the hills with their animals, traders came by lorry from three provinces, and on the open ground beyond the railway line a city of tents rose overnight.

(3) At noon the dancing began. A ring of drummers struck up a rhythm so fast and insistent that it seemed to come up through the soles of my feet, and a dozen camels, decorated with mirrors and tassels, began to sway and step in time. The mirrors flashed in the sun. The crowd roared its approval.

Text: The rising tide

(1) The rock pools at the far end of the beach were said to be the best on the whole coast, and on the last morning of our holiday in Cornwall my brother Omar and I went to find them. The tide was far out. The sand stretched away, ribbed and shining, to a line of surf so distant that it made no sound.

(2) We spent an hour crouched over the pools, absorbed. There were crabs that sidled away from our shadows, anemones like blobs of red jelly, and tiny fish that flicked between the weed too fast to follow. Omar found a starfish and named it Gerald. Neither of us looked up.

(3) When I finally did, the sea was no longer distant. It was racing towards us across the flat sand in long, shallow sheets, each wave sliding further than the last, and it had already filled the gully behind us, the gully we had crossed, dry-footed, an hour before. The rocks we stood on had become an island.

(4) I grabbed Omar's hand. The water in the gully was grey and rising and pulling sideways with surprising strength, and the far side, where the beach began, suddenly looked a very long way off. Omar's hand was cold in mine. He had stopped talking, which frightened me more than anything.

(5) We waded across up to our waists, the current tugging at our legs, our shoes held above our heads. On the beach a man walking his dog had seen everything; he said nothing, but he waited until we were safe before he walked on. We never told our parents. Gerald, I am fairly sure, was fine.

Text: Left behind

(1) Every day, at one of Europe's busiest railway stations, around four hundred objects are left behind. Most are predictable: umbrellas, scarves, phones, single gloves. But the staff of the lost-property office have also received a wedding dress, a set of false teeth, a full-size cello and, on one memorable morning, a live tortoise in a shoebox.

(2) Each item is logged within an hour of arriving. A clerk records where and when it was found, photographs it and gives it a numbered label. Valuable items such as laptops, passports and jewellery are locked in a safe, while food is thrown away at the end of the day for reasons of hygiene. Everything else is stored on metal shelves that run, floor to ceiling, through three underground rooms.

(3) Reuniting owners with their belongings is harder than it sounds. Many travellers do not realise what they have lost until they are hundreds of kilometres away, and by then they cannot remember which train they were on. Descriptions are often vague: 'a black bag' could match two hundred bags on the shelves. Staff therefore ask owners for one detail that only the true owner would know, such as a name written inside a book or the contents of a coat pocket.

(4) Items are kept for ninety days. After that, unclaimed goods are sold at auction, given to charities or, if they contain personal data, destroyed securely. Umbrellas, which are almost never collected, go to a shelter for homeless people.

(5) The staff admit that some returns stay with them. One clerk remembers an elderly man who had lost the only photograph of his late wife. When it was found tucked inside a timetable, he wept at the counter. 'People think we look after things,' she says. 'Really, we look after memories.'

Text: Seeds for the future

(1) In a small brick room behind a primary school near Okara, hundreds of glass jars stand in neat rows, each one labelled in careful handwriting. They contain seeds: wheat, millet, chickpeas, pumpkins, chillies, okra. Some of the varieties have been grown in local villages for generations and cannot be bought in any shop.

(2) The seed library was started eight years ago by a retired agriculture teacher, Ghulam Rasool, who noticed that the old varieties were quietly disappearing. Farmers had switched to modern seeds that gave bigger harvests in good years, but these often needed expensive fertiliser and plenty of water. When the canal ran low or the summer was unusually hot, the new crops sometimes failed completely, while the old ones, which had adapted to local conditions over centuries, usually survived.

(3) The library works like a book library. A farmer borrows a small bag of seed at planting time, grows the crop, and after the harvest returns twice as much seed as he or she took. In this way the collection grows every year without costing anything, and the seeds are constantly renewed. This matters, because seeds that sit in a jar for too long lose their ability to sprout.

(4) Not everyone was convinced at first. Some younger farmers dismissed the old varieties as backward. The turning point came after a drought four years ago, when the fields planted with borrowed seed gave a modest but reliable harvest and many neighbouring fields gave almost nothing.

(5) Today the library has more than three hundred members. Pupils from the school help to clean and label the seeds, and every spring a seed fair draws visitors from across the district. Rasool says his aim is simple: 'A seed that nobody plants is a seed that is already dying.'

parts.text: Using paragraph 2, explain why relying on modern seeds can be risky for farmers.
parts.answer: Modern seeds only give bigger crops in good years; they need costly fertiliser and a lot of water, so when water is short or it is very hot they can fail entirely, unlike old varieties that suit local conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: high yields only in good years; need expensive fertiliser (cost); need plenty of water; can fail completely when canal runs low / in drought; or in unusually hot summers; old varieties adapted to local conditions and usually survive (contrast).

parts.text: Using paragraph 3, explain how the seed library keeps its collection healthy without spending money.

parts.working: 1 mark each for: borrowing at planting time and returning twice as much after harvest; so the collection grows every year at no cost; seeds constantly renewed / replaced with fresh seed, which matters because stored seed loses its ability to sprout.

Text: Tape-ball nights

(1) During Ramadan in Karachi, the city keeps unusual hours. Long after the evening meal, when the heat has finally eased, the side streets fill with young men in shalwar kameez, floodlights strung from balconies and the sharp crack of a tennis ball wrapped in electrical tape striking a bat.

(2) Tape-ball cricket began as a cheap alternative to the real thing. A proper leather cricket ball is expensive and hard, and needs pads, gloves and a carefully prepared pitch. A tennis ball costs a fraction of the price, but on its own it is too light to be bowled fast. Wrapping it in tape makes it heavier and gives it a smooth, shiny surface, so bowlers can make it swing and skid without anyone needing protective equipment.

(3) The night tournaments are organised by neighbourhood committees. Teams pay a small entry fee, and the winners take home a trophy, a goat or, in recent years, a motorbike. Matches are short, usually six or eight overs a side, so a whole knockout tournament can be completed before the pre-dawn meal at about three in the morning.

(4) The game has produced some real stars. Several bowlers who learned their skills on tape-ball streets have gone on to play professional cricket, and coaches say the format teaches valuable lessons: bowlers learn to vary their pace and aim precisely, and batters learn to score quickly from the very first ball.

(5) Not everyone is a fan. Residents complain about the noise, and broken windows are a regular hazard. Yet many older people defend the tournaments, saying that the late-night games keep young people together, occupied and out of trouble during the holy month.

Text: The paper doctors

(1) In a quiet room on the top floor of a national library, a woman in a white coat is mending a book that is four hundred years old. She is not a doctor, but she talks about her work as if she were. 'Every book that comes to us is a patient,' she says. 'First we diagnose, then we treat, and above all we try to do no harm.'

(2) The diagnosis can take days. Conservators examine each page under different kinds of light, measure how acidic the paper is and note every tear, stain and wormhole. Old paper is often brittle, so even turning a page can cause damage. Each problem is photographed and written down before any work begins, so that future conservators can see exactly what was done.

(3) The treatments are slow and delicate. Tears are repaired with strips of thin Japanese paper, which is strong but almost transparent, and attached with a paste made from wheat starch. This paste is chosen because it can be removed later with a little water if a better method is discovered. Mould is brushed away by hand, and pages that have become acidic may be washed in special baths to make them last longer.

(4) Conservators follow one golden rule: anything they add must be reversible. Earlier generations sometimes used sticky tape or strong glues that turned yellow and destroyed the very pages they were meant to protect. Undoing these well-meant repairs is now a large part of the job.

(5) The work is rarely glamorous, and a single volume can take a year. But the conservator does not mind. 'These books have survived wars, floods and fires,' she says. 'It would be a shame to lose them to impatience.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using paragraph 2, explain why conservators take so much care before they begin any treatment.
parts.answer: Old paper is fragile, so careless handling could cause new damage; they need to know exactly what is wrong (light, acidity, every tear and hole), and they record everything so that later conservators know what was done.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: paper is brittle – even turning a page can damage it; must understand all the problems first (examine under different lights / measure acidity / note tears, stains, wormholes); everything photographed and recorded; so future conservators can see exactly what was done; (link to 'do no harm' – careful diagnosis avoids harm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using paragraphs 3 and 4, explain why conservators choose Japanese paper and wheat-starch paste for repairs.
parts.answer: The paper is strong yet nearly see-through, so the repair holds without hiding the text, and the paste can be washed off with water, so every repair can be undone if a better method appears, unlike old tapes and glues that yellowed and damaged pages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: Japanese paper is strong; almost transparent (does not hide the page); paste can be removed with a little water; repairs must be reversible / can be undone if a better method is found; avoids the damage caused by earlier tape and glue that yellowed / destroyed pages.

Text: Rebuilding the reef

(1) Twenty metres below the surface off a small island in the Indian Ocean, a marine biologist is hanging pieces of coral on what looks like a washing line. The 'line' is a rope stretched between two metal posts, and each fragment, no bigger than a finger, is tied on with a strip of fishing line. In a year, if all goes well, each one will be the size of a football.

(2) Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, yet they are home to around a quarter of all marine species. They protect coastlines by breaking the force of waves, and in many island nations they support fishing and tourism. But reefs are in trouble. When the sea becomes too warm, corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them and give them their colour and much of their food. The coral turns white, a process known as bleaching, and if the heat lasts too long, it dies.

(3) Coral gardening is one response. Fragments are collected from healthy colonies, often pieces that have already broken off naturally, and grown in underwater nurseries where they can be watched and cleaned. Once they are large enough, divers attach them to damaged parts of the reef with a type of cement that sets under water.

(4) Scientists are now trying to grow corals that can cope with warmer water. By selecting fragments from colonies that survived previous heatwaves, they hope to give restored reefs a better chance.

(5) Even supporters admit that coral gardening has limits. It is slow and expensive, and the area that can be replanted is tiny compared with the area that is being lost. 'We are buying time,' says the biologist. 'Only cutting the emissions that warm the ocean will truly save reefs.'

parts.text: Using paragraph 2, explain why warmer seas are harmful to coral.

Text: Where hands do the talking

(1) The classroom is noisy in its own way. Chairs scrape, a pencil drops, a child laughs. But the lesson itself happens in silence, in the swift movements of hands. At this school for deaf children in Rawalpindi, every subject, from mathematics to history, is taught in Pakistan Sign Language.

(5) The headteacher's biggest frustration is how much depends on chance. A deaf child born in a city near a school like this one may thrive; a child in a distant village may never meet another person who signs. She wants sign language taught in teacher-training colleges, so that every school has at least one teacher who can use it.

Text: Mud walls, cool rooms

(1) For thousands of years, people in hot, dry places have built their homes from the ground beneath their feet. In the villages of the Thar desert, round huts of mud and straw stay surprisingly cool even when the temperature outside passes forty-five degrees. Now architects in many countries are taking a fresh look at this ancient material.

(2) The secret lies in the thickness of the walls. Earth absorbs heat slowly during the day and releases it slowly at night, so the inside of a mud house changes temperature far less than the air outside. A concrete house of the same size, by contrast, can become an oven in the afternoon and need an air conditioner to stay comfortable.

(3) Earth also has environmental advantages. Making cement uses large amounts of energy and releases a great deal of carbon dioxide, whereas soil can often be dug on the building site itself and needs no factory at all. When an earth building is no longer wanted, its walls can simply return to the ground.

(4) The material does have weaknesses. Heavy rain can wash unprotected walls away, so earth buildings need wide roofs and a raised base of stone or brick to keep the walls dry. Earth is also less strong than reinforced concrete, which limits how tall a building can be, and in areas with earthquakes it must be carefully reinforced.

(5) The biggest obstacle, however, may be attitudes. In many places mud houses are seen as a sign of poverty, and families save for years to replace them with concrete. Architects who promote earth building say their first task is to show that it can be modern, beautiful and something to be proud of.

parts.text: Using paragraph 2, explain why mud houses stay cooler than concrete houses.

Text: The paper doctors

(1) In a quiet room on the top floor of a national library, a woman in a white coat is mending a book that is four hundred years old. She is not a doctor, but she talks about her work as if she were. 'Every book that comes to us is a patient,' she says. 'First we diagnose, then we treat, and above all we try to do no harm.'

(2) The diagnosis can take days. Conservators examine each page under different kinds of light, measure how acidic the paper is and note every tear, stain and wormhole. (3) The treatments are slow and delicate. Tears are repaired with strips of thin Japanese paper, which is strong but almost transparent, and attached with a paste made from wheat starch. This paste is chosen because it can be removed later with a little water if a better method is discovered. Mould is brushed away by hand, and pages that have become acidic may be washed in special baths to make them last longer.

(4) Conservators follow one golden rule: anything they add must be reversible. Earlier generations sometimes used sticky tape or strong glues that turned yellow and destroyed the very pages they were meant to protect. Undoing these well-meant repairs is now a large part of the job.

(5) The work is rarely glamorous, and a single volume can take a year. But the conservator does not mind. 'These books have survived wars, floods and fires,' she says. 'It would be a shame to lose them to impatience.'

Text: Mud walls, cool rooms

(1) For thousands of years, people in hot, dry places have built their homes from the ground beneath their feet. In the villages of the Thar desert, round huts of mud and straw stay surprisingly cool even when the temperature outside passes forty-five degrees. Now architects in many countries are taking a fresh look at this ancient material.

(2) The secret lies in the thickness of the walls. Earth absorbs heat slowly during the day and releases it slowly at night, so the inside of a mud house changes temperature far less than the air outside. A concrete house of the same size, by contrast, can become an oven in the afternoon and need an air conditioner to stay comfortable.

(3) Earth also has environmental advantages. Making cement uses large amounts of energy and releases a great deal of carbon dioxide, whereas soil can often be dug on the building site itself and needs no factory at all. When an earth building is no longer wanted, its walls can simply return to the ground.

(4) The material does have weaknesses. Heavy rain can wash unprotected walls away, so earth buildings need wide roofs and a raised base of stone or brick to keep the walls dry. Earth is also less strong than reinforced concrete, which limits how tall a building can be, and in areas with earthquakes it must be carefully reinforced.

(5) The biggest obstacle, however, may be attitudes. In many places mud houses are seen as a sign of poverty, and families save for years to replace them with concrete. Architects who promote earth building say their first task is to show that it can be modern, beautiful and something to be proud of.

(2) The diagnosis can take days. Conservators examine each page under different kinds of light, measure how acidic the paper is and note every tear, stain and wormhole. Old paper is often brittle, so even turning a page can cause damage. Each problem is photographed and written down before any work begins, so that future conservators can see exactly what was done.

(3) The treatments are slow and delicate. Tears are repaired with strips of thin Japanese paper, which is strong but almost transparent, and attached with a paste made from wheat starch. This paste is chosen because it can be removed later with a little water if a better method is discovered. Mould is brushed away by hand, and pages that have become acidic may be washed in special baths to make them last longer.

(4) Conservators follow one golden rule: anything they add must be reversible. Earlier generations sometimes used sticky tape or strong glues that turned yellow and destroyed the very pages they were meant to protect. Undoing these well-meant repairs is now a large part of the job.

(5) The work is rarely glamorous, and a single volume can take a year. But the conservator does not mind. 'These books have survived wars, floods and fires,' she says. 'It would be a shame to lose them to impatience.'

(4) Scientists are now trying to grow corals that can cope with warmer water. By selecting fragments from colonies that survived previous heatwaves, they hope to give restored reefs a better chance.

(5) Even supporters admit that coral gardening has limits. It is slow and expensive, and the area that can be replanted is tiny compared with the area that is being lost. 'We are buying time,' says the biologist. 'Only cutting the emissions that warm the ocean will truly save reefs.'

Text: Mud walls, cool rooms

(1) For thousands of years, people in hot, dry places have built their homes from the ground beneath their feet. In the villages of the Thar desert, round huts of mud and straw stay surprisingly cool even when the temperature outside passes forty-five degrees. Now architects in many countries are taking a fresh look at this ancient material.

(2) The secret lies in the thickness of the walls. Earth absorbs heat slowly during the day and releases it slowly at night, so the inside of a mud house changes temperature far less than the air outside. A concrete house of the same size, by contrast, can become an oven in the afternoon and need an air conditioner to stay comfortable.

(3) Earth also has environmental advantages. Making cement uses large amounts of energy and releases a great deal of carbon dioxide, whereas soil can often be dug on the building site itself and needs no factory at all. When an earth building is no longer wanted, its walls can simply return to the ground.

(4) The material does have weaknesses. Heavy rain can wash unprotected walls away, so earth buildings need wide roofs and a raised base of stone or brick to keep the walls dry. Earth is also less strong than reinforced concrete, which limits how tall a building can be, and in areas with earthquakes it must be carefully reinforced.

(5) The biggest obstacle, however, may be attitudes. In many places mud houses are seen as a sign of poverty, and families save for years to replace them with concrete. Architects who promote earth building say their first task is to show that it can be modern, beautiful and something to be proud of.

(5) Nobody pretends that herders now love snow leopards. But attitudes have softened. Some young people from the valley now work as guides, taking visitors on winter treks in the hope of glimpsing a cat. 'Once it was our enemy,' says one herder. First, I learned how a hospital really works. I saw how nurses hand over patients at the change of shift, how carefully medicines are checked, and how many people, from cleaners to porters, are needed to keep a single ward running. It made me understand why every job matters.

Text: Three generations under one roof

In much of South Asia the joint family, with grandparents, parents and children sharing a home, is still common, although many young couples now dream of a flat of their own. Researchers who have studied such households say that, for all their arguments over the television, they offer advantages that are easy to overlook.

The most obvious is shared cost. Rent, electricity and food are divided among several earners, so each pays less than they would living alone, and expensive items such as a car or a refrigerator can be bought together.

Childcare is the second. When both parents work, grandparents are often at home, which means children come back from school to a familiar face rather than an empty house or a paid stranger. Many parents say this is the only reason both of them can hold full-time jobs.

The benefits flow in both directions. Older people who live with their families are less likely to be lonely, and if they fall ill there is always someone to notice, to fetch medicine or to take them to a doctor.

Children in joint families grow up surrounded by different generations. They hear stories of the past, learn the language and customs of their grandparents, and pick up practical skills, from cooking to repairing a bicycle, from whichever relative happens to be around. They also learn, through daily practice, to share, to compromise and to respect people whose opinions differ from their own.

Finally, in a crisis, a joint family acts like a safety net. If someone loses a job or is injured, the household can absorb the shock together, rather than one person facing it alone.

Text: Tomatoes on the balcony

You do not need a garden to grow your own tomatoes. A sunny balcony, or even a wide windowsill, is enough, as long as you follow a few simple rules.

Start with the right container. Tomato plants have deep roots, so choose a pot at least thirty centimetres deep, and make sure it has holes in the bottom so that extra water can drain away. Fill it with good-quality compost rather than soil dug from the street, which may be poor or contain pests.

Position matters more than anything else. Tomatoes need at least six hours of direct sunlight a day, so place the pot where it gets the most sun, and turn it every week so that the plant does not lean towards the light.

Water deeply but not too often. A thorough soaking two or three times a week is better than a splash every day, and it is best done in the early morning, before the heat of the day. In very hot weather, a layer of dried leaves or straw on top of the compost keeps the moisture in.

As the plant grows, tie it gently to a stick or cane so that the stem does not snap under the weight of the fruit. Pinch out the small side shoots that grow between the main stem and the branches; this sends the plant's energy into the fruit.

Once the first flowers appear, feed the plant every week with a liquid tomato fertiliser. Finally, be patient. Pick the tomatoes only when they are fully coloured, and enjoy a flavour no shop can match.

Text: Beating the mosquito

Every monsoon, cases of dengue fever rise sharply in many South Asian cities. The disease is spread by mosquitoes that bite mainly during the day, and there is no simple cure, so prevention is everything. Fortunately, there is a great deal that families can do.

The most important step is to stop mosquitoes breeding. They lay their eggs in clean, still water, and a bottle cap of water is enough. Once a week, empty and scrub flower-pot saucers, buckets and pet bowls, and cover water tanks tightly. Old tyres and broken pots on rooftops should be thrown away or turned upside down.

Next, keep mosquitoes out of the house. Fit fine mesh screens to windows and doors, and repair any holes. If screens are not possible, keep doors closed during the day, especially in the early morning and late afternoon, when these mosquitoes are most active.

Protect your body as well. Long sleeves and long trousers leave less skin exposed, and insect repellent should be applied to any skin that is uncovered, following the instructions on the label. Babies and young children who nap during the day should sleep under a mosquito net.

Communities can do even more by working together. Neighbours who organise clean-up days to clear rubbish and blocked drains remove breeding sites that no single family could reach.

Finally, know the warning signs. Anyone with a high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes or aching joints should see a doctor quickly rather than waiting to see whether it passes.

Text: The town that said no to plastic bags

Five years ago, a small market town in Sindh, like most towns, was drowning in plastic bags. They hung from trees, blocked drains during the rains and were found in the stomachs of stray cattle. Today they are rare. The change did not happen by accident.

It began with the traders. The market association agreed that its members would stop giving out free plastic bags on a single date, so that no shop could lose customers to a rival that still offered them.

At the same time, alternatives were made cheap and easy. A local women's cooperative began sewing strong cloth bags from offcuts supplied by a textile mill, and these were sold at stalls for less than the price of a cup of tea. Shopkeepers kept a few to lend to customers who had forgotten theirs.

Schools played a vital role. Pupils studied the effects of plastic on animals and drains, painted murals in the bazaar and, most effectively, went home and nagged their parents.

The town council made the change official with a by-law, but chose to enforce it gently at first, giving warnings rather than fines for the first six months while people adjusted.

Finally, everyone could see the results. Volunteers organised monthly clean-ups of the canal bank, and photographs of the cleaner streets and clear drains were displayed in the market. When people saw what they had achieved, few wanted to go back.

Text: When the river rises

In August three years ago, the river burst its banks and flooded the bazaar of a small town in southern Punjab to the height of a man's waist. Shopkeepers lost stock worth millions of rupees. When the waters rose again last year, the same shops lost almost nothing. What had changed?

First, the traders learned to listen for warnings. The town now has a flood committee that follows the official forecasts and passes on alerts to every shop by text message and by loudspeaker from the mosque, giving owners up to two days to prepare.

Shopkeepers also changed the way they store goods. Valuable stock is now kept on shelves at least a metre above the floor, and many shops have built a small concrete platform at the back where sacks of flour and rice can be stacked out of reach of the water.

Some have gone further. A few owners have bricked up the lower part of their shop doors and fitted removable wooden boards that slot into metal frames, which keep out shallow floods.

The traders also prepared their paperwork. Account books and important documents are now copied onto phones or stored in waterproof boxes, so that records of debts and payments are not lost.

The committee has also persuaded the council to clear the drains and the canal before every monsoon, so that water drains away more quickly.

Finally, the traders agreed to help one another. Each street has a group of young volunteers who move stock to the upper floors of a neighbouring school when a warning is issued, so that elderly shopkeepers are not left to struggle alone.

Text: What makes a good coach

Every Saturday morning, thousands of young people across the country turn up to train with volunteer football and cricket coaches. Some of these teenagers will play for years; others will give up within a season. Research into youth sport suggests that the coach, more than the facilities or the results, often makes the difference.

The best coaches, it seems, care more about improvement than about winning. They praise effort and progress, not just goals and wickets, so that weaker players do not feel worthless when the team loses.

They also know their players as individuals. A good coach notices who is struggling at school, who is anxious before matches and who needs a harder challenge, and adjusts what they say and ask accordingly.

Training sessions matter. Young people quickly lose interest if they spend half an hour standing in a queue, so effective coaches plan sessions in which everyone is active, using small groups and games rather than long lectures.

Fairness is essential. Players notice at once if the coach's favourites always get the most time on the pitch. The coaches who keep their teams together give every player a turn and explain clearly why selections are made.

Good coaches also set an example. They arrive on time, stay calm when a referee makes a poor decision and treat the opposing team with respect, and their players tend to copy them.

Finally, the best coaches keep learning themselves. They attend courses, watch other coaches and ask their players what they enjoy, and are not too proud to change what is not working.

Text: Life on the long-haul road

Every night on the motorway between Karachi and Peshawar, thousands of lorries carry fuel, cement, fruit and furniture across the country. For the drivers behind the wheel, the journey is anything but romantic.

The first problem is exhaustion. Drivers are often paid by the trip rather than by the hour, so many drive for sixteen hours or more with only short breaks. Tiredness slows their reactions, and a moment's sleep at the wheel can be fatal.

The roads themselves are dangerous. Some stretches are poorly lit, and overloaded lorries, broken-down vehicles without warning lights and animals wandering onto the road all cause accidents. In the hills, brakes can overheat on long descents.

Drivers also face crime. Lorries carrying valuable goods are sometimes stopped by gangs, and drivers who resist may be injured.

Their health suffers in other ways. Meals at roadside cafés are cheap but oily, and sitting for long hours causes back pain and weight gain. Few drivers have regular medical check-ups, so problems such as high blood pressure often go unnoticed.

Perhaps the hardest part is the time away from home. Drivers may not see their families for weeks, and many say they miss their children growing up. Loneliness on the long night hours is common.

Finally, the work is insecure. Most drivers do not own their lorries, have no written contract and receive no pension, so an accident or illness can leave a family without income.

Text: Into the fire

When wildfires spread through forests in the dry season, it is firefighters who stand between the flames and the villages beyond. Their work is among the most dangerous in the world.

The fire itself is unpredictable. A sudden change in the wind can turn a slow-moving fire into a fast one, and flames can race uphill far more quickly than a person can run. Firefighters can find themselves surrounded with little warning.

Heat is a danger even away from the flames. Crews work for hours in heavy protective clothing, often in summer temperatures above forty degrees, and heat exhaustion is a constant risk. They must carry litres of water, yet it is still easy to become dehydrated.

Smoke is another hazard. It irritates the eyes and lungs, makes it hard to see, and over years of exposure may damage firefighters' long-term health.

The ground is treacherous too. Burnt trees can fall without warning, loose rocks roll down slopes, and hidden holes where roots have burnt away can trap a foot.

Communication is difficult in remote hills, where radios may not work and crews can lose contact with one another.

Finally, the work is exhausting in a way that wears people down. Big fires can last for weeks, and crews may sleep only a few hours a night in temporary camps, far from their families. Many firefighters also describe the emotional strain of seeing homes destroyed and wildlife killed, despite all their efforts.

Text: The vanishing dark

Two hundred years ago, almost everyone on Earth could look up on a clear night and see the Milky Way. Today, because of artificial light, most people living in cities never see it at all. Light pollution, scientists say, is a growing problem that affects far more than stargazing.

Wildlife is badly affected. Many birds migrate at night and use the stars to find their way; bright cities confuse them, and millions die each year after flying into lit buildings. Newly hatched sea turtles, which head towards the brightest horizon, may crawl inland towards street lights instead of towards the sea. Insects circle lamps until they die of exhaustion, which in turn affects the birds and bats that feed on them.

People suffer too. Our bodies use darkness as a signal to produce the hormone that helps us sleep, and bright light at night, from street lamps outside the window as well as from screens, can disturb this natural rhythm. Poor sleep has been linked to a range of health problems.

Much outdoor light is simply wasted. Badly designed lamps shine upwards and sideways instead of down onto the street, so cities pay for electricity that lights up the sky. Producing that electricity often means burning fuel and releasing carbon dioxide.

There is a cultural loss as well. For thousands of years, people used the night sky to tell stories, to mark the seasons and to navigate. Children who grow up never seeing stars lose that connection.

Finally, astronomers find it harder and harder to work, as the glow from distant cities spreads into even remote observatories.

Text: The green carpet

From a distance, the lake looks like a meadow. A thick green carpet of water hyacinth stretches from the shore for hundreds of metres, its purple flowers bright in the sun. To the fishermen who depend on the lake, it is a disaster.

Water hyacinth is not native to the region. It was brought from South America as an ornamental plant, and in warm water rich in nutrients from farm fertiliser and sewage, it grows at astonishing speed, doubling its area in a couple of weeks.

The mats are so dense that boats cannot pass through them. Fishermen must spend hours cutting a way out each morning, and some landing places have been completely cut off. Nets become tangled in the roots.

Beneath the surface, the plant blocks sunlight and reduces the oxygen in the water as dead plants rot, so fish die or move away. Catches have fallen sharply.

The weed also causes problems far from the shore. It clogs the pumps that supply water to nearby towns and the intakes of a small hydroelectric plant, which have to be cleaned at great cost.

Standing water among the mats provides an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes, and health workers have reported more cases of malaria in lakeside villages.

Attempts to remove the plant have had little lasting effect. Cutting it by hand is slow and exhausting, machines are expensive, and every fragment left behind can grow into a new plant. Meanwhile, the nutrients from fields and towns that feed it continue to pour into the lake.

Text: Too loud to think

Cities have always been noisy, but researchers now say that the constant roar of modern urban life is a serious problem in its own right, not merely an annoyance.

Traffic is the main source. Car horns, motorcycles, buses and lorries produce a background noise that, on busy roads, rarely falls silent even at night. Construction sites, generators and loudspeakers add to it.

The most immediate effect is on sleep. People who live beside busy roads often wake many times in the night, sometimes without remembering it, and they wake up tired. Over time, poor sleep affects mood and concentration.

Noise also places strain on the body. Studies have found that people exposed to loud traffic for years are more likely to suffer from high blood pressure and heart disease, possibly because noise keeps the body in a constant state of mild stress.

Hearing itself can be damaged. Traffic police, shopkeepers and street vendors who spend all day beside main roads are at risk of permanent hearing loss.

Children are particularly affected. Pupils in schools close to airports or highways have been found to learn to read more slowly, because they find it harder to concentrate and teachers must keep raising their voices.

Noise affects relationships too. Arguments between neighbours over loud music or barking dogs are among the most common complaints received by city councils.

Finally, noise drives away wildlife. Birds in cities have been recorded singing louder and at higher pitch simply to be heard, and some species abandon noisy areas altogether.

Text: The road to secondary school

In many rural districts of Pakistan, almost as many girls as boys now start primary school. By the age of fourteen, however, far fewer girls are still in the classroom. Researchers who have spoken to families have found that the reasons are many, and they reinforce one another.

Distance is the most common barrier. A village may have a primary school but no secondary school, and the nearest one may be ten or fifteen kilometres away. Without safe, affordable transport, many parents are unwilling to let their daughters make the journey.

Safety concerns go beyond the road. Parents worry about harassment, and some schools lack a boundary wall or a separate toilet for girls, which matters greatly to families.

Money is another obstacle. Although government schools charge no fees, uniforms, books and transport cost more than many families can afford, and when money is short, boys' education is often given priority.

Girls are also needed at home. Older daughters look after younger brothers and sisters, fetch water and help in the fields, especially at harvest time, and this work makes regular attendance difficult.

There is a shortage of female teachers in rural areas, which some families see as essential for older girls.

Early marriage takes some girls out of school altogether.

Finally, some parents see little point in educating girls if there will be no jobs for them afterwards. Yet the research also found that where one girl from a village had gone on to become a teacher or health worker, other families quickly changed their minds.

Text: Above the clouds

Every summer, climbers from around the world travel to the Karakoram, home to several of the highest mountains on Earth. Reaching a summit above eight thousand metres is the achievement of a lifetime. It is also extraordinarily dangerous.

The greatest threat is the altitude itself. At such heights each breath contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level. Climbers become breathless, weak and confused, and some develop altitude sickness, in which fluid gathers in the lungs or brain. Without a rapid descent, this can kill within hours.

The weather is another enemy. Storms can arrive with little warning, bringing winds strong enough to knock a climber off a ridge and temperatures far below freezing. Frostbite can cost climbers their fingers and toes.

The mountains themselves are unstable. Avalanches sweep down slopes after heavy snow, and huge blocks of ice can break off glaciers without any warning. Hidden crevasses, deep cracks in the ice covered by a thin bridge of snow, can swallow a climber who is not roped to others.

Exhaustion makes all of these dangers worse. A summit day may last eighteen hours, and many accidents happen on the way down, when climbers are tired and their judgement is poor.

Rescue is extremely difficult. Helicopters cannot fly safely at the highest altitudes, and carrying an injured climber down steep ice takes many people and many hours.

Finally, there is the pressure of ambition. Climbers who have spent years of savings and months of training may refuse to turn back even when conditions are clearly unsafe.

Text: When the bank goes online

Over the past few years, many banks have closed local branches and moved their services online. For younger customers, banking by phone is quick and convenient. But for many elderly people, the change has created serious difficulties.

The most basic problem is access. Some older people do not own a smartphone or a computer, and others have no internet connection at home. Even those who do may find that their phone is too old to run the bank's app.

Passwords cause endless trouble. Banks require long, complicated passwords and codes sent by text message, and those who forget them can be locked out of their own accounts.

Older people are also targeted by fraudsters. Criminals send messages pretending to be from the bank, and people who are new to online banking find it hard to tell real messages from fake ones. Some have lost their life savings.

The closure of branches has a human cost too. For some older people, a weekly visit to the bank was a chance to talk to someone. Now the nearest branch may be an expensive bus journey away.

Finally, many feel embarrassed to ask for help. They depend on children or neighbours to manage their money, which can leave them feeling that they have lost their independence.

Text: Hens in the yard

Keeping a few chickens at home was once normal in villages and small towns, and it is becoming popular again, even in city houses with a small yard or roof. But anyone thinking of buying hens should consider both sides.

The most obvious advantage is fresh eggs. Three or four healthy hens can lay enough eggs for a family most days, saving money and providing eggs that are as fresh as possible.

Chickens also reduce waste. They eat vegetable peelings and leftover rice that would otherwise be thrown away, and their droppings make excellent fertiliser for a vegetable patch. They even eat insects and weeds.

Many parents say that chickens teach children responsibility, since the birds must be fed, watered and shut in every evening. Children also learn where food comes from.

And, as many owners discover, chickens can be surprisingly entertaining, each with its own personality.

There are, however, drawbacks. Chickens need daily care, so holidays require someone to look after them. They must be kept in a secure coop at night, because cats, dogs and other predators will kill them.

Chickens can be noisy, especially when they have laid an egg, and a cockerel crowing at dawn will not please the neighbours. If the coop is not cleaned regularly, it smells and attracts rats and flies.

Hens can also carry diseases, so hands must be washed carefully after handling them or their eggs.

Finally, hens lay fewer eggs as they grow older, and owners must decide what to do with birds that no longer lay.

Text: Charging ahead

Electric cars, once a rare sight, are now appearing on roads in many countries, and several governments plan to stop the sale of new petrol cars within the next twenty years. Supporters and sceptics disagree about how much good they will do.

The clearest advantage is cleaner air in cities. Electric cars produce no exhaust fumes, so streets crowded with them would be far healthier for pedestrians, especially children and people with asthma.

They are also cheaper to run. Charging a battery usually costs much less than filling a tank with petrol, and because electric motors have far fewer moving parts than engines, they need less servicing.

Drivers often enjoy them. Electric cars are almost silent and accelerate smoothly, which makes city driving more relaxing.

If the electricity comes from solar, wind or water power, an electric car's contribution to climate change can be much lower than that of a petrol car.

There are, however, real disadvantages. Electric cars are expensive to buy, largely because of the cost of the battery, putting them out of reach of many families.

Charging is a problem in many places. Public charging points are still scarce outside big cities, a full charge can take hours, and people who live in flats without parking may have nowhere to plug in.

The batteries themselves raise concerns. Mining the metals they contain can damage the environment and the health of workers, and recycling old batteries is still difficult.

Finally, where electricity is generated by burning coal or oil, the benefit to the climate is much smaller, and in countries with frequent power cuts, relying on the electricity supply to travel may be risky.

Text: Turning in the wind

On a ridge above the coast in Sindh, a line of white wind turbines turns slowly against the sky. Wind farms like this one are being built across the world as countries look for cleaner sources of electricity. Not everyone welcomes them.

Their main advantage is that they generate electricity without burning fuel, so they produce no smoke and very little carbon dioxide once they are built. The wind is free and will never run out.

Wildlife can be harmed. Birds and bats are sometimes killed by the turning blades, particularly if turbines are built on migration routes.

Finally, the best sites for wind are often far from cities, so new power lines must be built to carry the electricity, which is costly. Building the turbines also requires large amounts of steel and concrete.

Text: Should the long holiday be shorter?

In many countries, schools close for two or three months in summer. Some educators now argue that the year should be reorganised, with a shorter summer break and more frequent short holidays spread across the year. The idea has supporters and opponents.

Child stars have existed as long as films and television, but social media has multiplied their number. Text: The greatest show on Earth?

When a city wins the right to host the Olympic Games or a football World Cup, crowds celebrate in the streets. Years later, the verdict is often less clear. Economists who have studied major sporting events have found both real gains and heavy costs.

On the positive side, hosting brings visitors. Hundreds of thousands of fans fill hotels, restaurants and shops during the event, and the worldwide television coverage can advertise the host city to future tourists for years.

The event itself can disrupt ordinary life, with closed roads and higher prices for local people. In some cases poorer residents have been forced out of their homes to make way for new venues.

Even the tourist boom can be disappointing: regular visitors often avoid a city during a major event because of crowds and expense, and the expected surge in sports participation does not always last.

Text: Drinking the sea

As rivers shrink and underground water is pumped faster than rain can replace it, more and more coastal cities are turning to the sea for drinking water. Desalination plants remove the salt from seawater, usually by forcing it at high pressure through very fine membranes. The technology is proven, but it is not a perfect answer.

Its great advantage is reliability. The sea does not run dry in a drought, so a desalination plant can supply water whatever the weather, which is why it is used in desert countries with almost no rainfall.

It can also take pressure off rivers and underground water, allowing these sources to recover, and it reduces conflict between farmers, industries and cities competing for the same supply.

The water produced is of high quality, and the cost of desalination has fallen considerably in recent decades as the technology has improved.

However, desalination uses large amounts of energy, which makes the water expensive and, if the energy comes from burning fossil fuels, adds to climate change.

For every litre of fresh water produced, the process leaves behind a very salty liquid called brine, which is usually pumped back into the sea. Released carelessly, it can harm fish, corals and other sea life near the outlet.

Building a plant costs a great deal of money and takes years, which many poorer cities cannot afford. And because the plants must be on the coast, piping the water to inland towns adds further cost.

Finally, some environmentalists fear that cheap, plentiful water from the sea may discourage people from saving water at all.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about replacing the library's printed books with tablets
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Headteacher'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – writing as a regular library user in response to the plan. Para 2 – Text A's practical points (no lost or damaged books, adjustable text, instant dictionary) are real, but the claim that paper books 'belong to the last century' is a sales brochure's exaggeration. Para 3 – Text B's points on power cuts, broken devices and distraction are practical problems A ignores; eye strain concerns add weight. Para 4 – the value of browsing and of a librarian's advice (B) cannot be measured by A's reading statistics. Para 5 – own view: keep the library and librarian, add a small number of e-readers for reference and large-print needs; ask pupils' views. Formal close.
parts.working: Ideas to evaluate: Text A: tablets give thousands of books for the price of a few hundred; e-books never lost, torn or on loan; adjustable text size; instant dictionary; portable; teachers can track reading; freed space for a modern study area. Text B: browsing shelves creates a love of reading; tablets break, batteries die; power cuts; children already overuse screens – eyes and sleep; risk of games instead of reading; library as quiet, safe space; librarian recommends suitable books. Evaluation points: A is written by a company that sells the technology – biased; it says nothing about cost of repairs or power cuts. B is from experience but may be nostalgic; still, her practical objections are strong. Monitoring reading (A) may feel intrusive. A balanced solution is possible. Register: formal and polite, persuasive, with a clear purpose in the opening and a courteous close. author: HomiLabs

stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Widen the road now (from a city traffic department notice)

Canal Road carries twice the traffic it was built for. At peak times, a journey of four kilometres can take forty minutes, ambulances are trapped in the queues and the fumes from idling engines hang over the homes on either side.

The city plans to widen the road from two lanes to four in each direction. To do so, the row of old trees along the central strip must be removed. New saplings will be planted elsewhere in the city to replace every tree that is cut down.

Faster journeys will save fuel, cut pollution and help businesses. We ask residents for their patience during construction.

Text B: The trees are the city's lungs (from a residents' group leaflet)

The trees along Canal Road are more than a hundred years old. In summer they shade the road and the pavements, lowering the temperature by several degrees, and they absorb dust and noise from the traffic.

A sapling planted somewhere else will take decades to give the same shade, and many newly planted trees die in the first hot summer without care.

Every city that has widened its roads has found the same thing: within a few years, the new lanes fill up with even more cars. The real answer is better buses and safe routes for walking and cycling, not more space for traffic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your city council is planning to cut down a row of old trees in order to widen a busy road. You decide to write a letter to the council.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about cutting down the trees to widen the road
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Sir or Madam'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – resident writing about the proposal. Para 2 – acknowledge the real traffic problem in Text A: long journeys, ambulances delayed, fumes. Para 3 – question A's promise of replacement saplings using B's point that young trees take decades and often die. Para 4 – evaluate the claim that faster journeys reduce pollution against B's argument that wider roads attract more cars. Para 5 – own view: keep the trees; invest in buses, ambulance priority lanes and cycling routes; if any widening is essential, design it around the trees. Formal close requesting a public consultation.
parts.working: Ideas to evaluate: Text A: road carries double the traffic; 40-minute journeys; ambulances stuck; fumes for residents; widen to four lanes; trees must go; saplings planted elsewhere; faster journeys save fuel, cut pollution, help business. Text B: trees over 100 years old; shade lowers temperature; absorb dust and noise; saplings take decades and often die; wider roads fill with more cars; better buses, walking and cycling are the answer. Evaluation points: Both agree the traffic is a problem. A's pollution claim ignores B's point about extra traffic. A's 'replacement' is not like for like. B offers alternatives but does not explain how ambulances would get through now. A compromise (bus lanes, ambulance priority) uses both texts. Register: formal and polite, persuasive, with a clear purpose in the opening and a courteous close. stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Faster checkouts for everyone (from a supermarket chain's announcement to staff)

From next month, our branches will install self-checkout machines. Customers will scan and pay for their own shopping, cutting waiting times at busy periods by up to half.

Our research shows that many younger shoppers prefer to serve themselves, and the machines are available whenever the store is open.

No staff member will lose their job. Cashiers will be retrained as 'customer hosts', helping shoppers on the shop floor, restocking shelves and assisting at the machines. The savings will help us keep our prices low at a time when every family is feeling the cost of living.

Text B: Machines don't smile (a blog post by a shop worker)

I have worked on a supermarket till for six years. Many of my customers are elderly or live alone, and the few minutes we spend chatting while I scan their shopping may be the only conversation they have all day.

Self-checkouts are not as quick as the companies claim. They freeze, flash error messages about 'unexpected items' and need a member of staff to sort them out. Older customers and those who cannot read well often give up and leave.

Companies always promise that nobody will lose their job. But once the machines are installed, fewer people are hired to replace those who leave, and the 'hosts' are spread more and more thinly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
You work part-time at a supermarket. The manager has announced that most cashiers' tills will be replaced with self-checkout machines. You decide to write a letter to the manager.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about replacing cashiers with self-checkout machines
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Manager'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – part-time employee writing respectfully about the announcement. Para 2 – recognise the benefits in Text A: shorter queues, customer choice, lower prices – but note that the 'up to half' figure is the company's own research. Para 3 – evaluate A's promise of no job losses against B's warning about not replacing staff who leave. Para 4 – B's points about lonely and elderly customers and malfunctioning machines show what figures miss. Para 5 – own view: install some machines but keep staffed tills, especially at quieter times for older customers; train hosts properly; review after six months with customer feedback. Formal close.
parts.working: Ideas to evaluate: Text A: queues cut by up to half; younger shoppers prefer it; always available; no job losses; cashiers retrained as hosts; savings keep prices low. Text B: tills provide conversation for lonely or elderly customers; machines freeze and show errors; need staff anyway; older or less literate customers give up; jobs disappear gradually as leavers are not replaced; hosts spread thinly. Evaluation points: A's claims are self-interested and partly unproven; B is based on experience but is one worker's view. Both want good service. Retraining is positive if genuine. A mixed system addresses both sides. Register: formal and polite, persuasive, with a clear purpose in the opening and a courteous close. stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: A healthier canteen (from a school health committee's proposal)

One in five pupils at our school is overweight, and the school nurse sees more children each year with tooth decay. We believe the canteen is part of the problem.

We propose that from next term the canteen stops selling fizzy drinks, crisps and fried snacks. Instead, it will offer fruit, plain water, milk, lentil dishes and wholemeal sandwiches at the same prices.

Schools that have made this change report that pupils concentrate better in afternoon lessons. Children learn their eating habits young, and a school that teaches healthy living in science lessons should not sell junk food at lunchtime.

Text B: Let us choose (from a student newspaper)

Nobody disagrees that fruit is healthier than crisps. But banning snacks in the canteen will not stop anyone eating them: there are three shops outside the school gate, and they will be delighted to take the canteen's customers.

The canteen uses its profits to help pay for sports equipment and trips. If sales fall, those activities will suffer.

Many of us are old enough to make our own decisions, and lecturing teenagers usually makes them do the opposite. A better approach would be to make healthy food cheaper and tastier, label everything clearly, and leave the choice to us.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your school is considering banning sugary drinks and fried snacks from the school canteen. You decide to write a letter to the headteacher.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about banning sugary drinks and fried snacks in the canteen
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Headteacher'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – student writing about the proposal. Para 2 – Text A's health evidence (weight, tooth decay) is serious and the school's credibility point is persuasive. Para 3 – Text B's practical objection (shops at the gate) weakens the idea that a ban alone changes habits; loss of canteen profits matters for sport. Para 4 – weigh B's 'respect our choices' against A's point that habits form young. Para 5 – own view: phase out fizzy drinks, keep a few snacks but make healthy food cheaper and more appealing; involve pupils in choosing the menu; education alongside change. Formal close.
parts.working: Ideas to evaluate: Text A: one in five overweight; more tooth decay; ban fizzy drinks, crisps, fried snacks; offer fruit, water, milk, lentils, wholemeal at same prices; better afternoon concentration; habits formed young; school should practise what it teaches. Text B: agrees fruit healthier; pupils will buy from shops outside; canteen profits fund sport and trips; teenagers can choose; lecturing backfires; make healthy food cheaper and tastier; clear labels. Evaluation points: A uses statistics and reports from other schools (unnamed); B raises practical consequences A ignores. B's 'we can choose' may be true for older pupils but not younger ones. Both want healthier pupils; disagreement is about method. Register: formal and polite, persuasive, with a clear purpose in the opening and a courteous close. stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Cameras keep us safe (from a city police statement)

Following a rise in phone snatching and vandalism, the city plans to install closed-circuit television cameras in all public parks. The cameras will be monitored from a central control room twenty-four hours a day.

Where cameras have been installed in the main bazaar, street crime has fallen by a third. Families tell us they feel more confident letting children play outside when they know someone is watching. Recordings also help police identify offenders and provide evidence in court.

Law-abiding citizens have nothing to fear from cameras. Only those planning to commit crimes need worry.

Text B: Parks are not prisons (from a civil rights group's website)

A park should be a place where people can relax, talk privately and be themselves. Constant filming changes that. Young couples, women who simply want to sit alone and people meeting friends will all feel watched.

Cameras do not prevent crime so much as move it: when one area is filmed, offenders simply go elsewhere. Many crimes are over in seconds, long before police can arrive.

And who will see the recordings? Without strict rules, footage can be misused or leaked. The money would be better spent on lighting, park wardens and youth activities, which tackle the causes of crime rather than just recording it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Your city council is considering installing CCTV cameras in all public parks. You decide to write a letter to the council.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about installing CCTV cameras in public parks
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Sir or Madam'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – resident and park user. Para 2 – Text A's evidence (crime down by a third in the bazaar) is persuasive but a bazaar is not a park; does the figure prove cause? Para 3 – B's displacement argument and the speed of crimes weaken A's claims; but recordings as evidence (A) are a fair point. Para 4 – evaluate A's 'nothing to fear' against B's concerns about privacy and misuse; argue the slogan avoids the real question of who controls footage. Para 5 – own view: cameras only at entrances and car parks, strict rules on access and deletion, plus lighting and wardens; review crime figures after a year. Formal close.

Text B: parks for relaxation and privacy; filming makes people feel watched (couples, women alone); cameras displace crime; crimes over in seconds; risk of misuse or leaks; spend on lighting, wardens, youth activities to tackle causes. Evaluation points: A's statistic is from a different setting; 'nothing to fear' is a slogan, not an argument. B's privacy concerns are real but it offers little evidence that its alternatives work.
