stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Measure what matters (from a software company's advertisement)

Do you really know how your team spends its working day? Our monitoring software records which programs and websites employees use, how long they are active at the keyboard and when they take breaks.

Managers receive a clear weekly report showing who is most productive. Companies using our product report a fifteen per cent rise in output within three months, because staff who know their time is recorded waste less of it.

The software also protects your business: it can alert you if confidential files are copied or sent outside the company.

Text B: Trust, not tracking (from an article by a workplace psychologist)

Measuring keyboard activity tells you nothing about the quality of someone's work. A designer staring out of the window may be solving a difficult problem; a clerk typing all day may be doing something pointless.

Workers who feel constantly watched become anxious and resentful. Some find ways to look busy, such as moving the mouse regularly, rather than doing better work. Good employees often leave for companies that treat them as adults.

Managers who want productive teams should set clear goals, judge people by results and talk to them regularly. Surveillance is a poor substitute for leadership.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The company where you work is planning to install software that records employees' computer activity. You decide to write a letter to the managing director.

In your letter you should:
• evaluate the views given in both texts about monitoring employees' computer activity
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

Begin your letter, 'Dear Managing Director'.

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words. Address both of the bullet points. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 25 marks for the quality of your writing (exam total 40).
parts.answer: Model plan: Opening – employee writing about the planned software. Para 2 – Text A's security point (copying confidential files) is legitimate and separate from productivity tracking. Para 3 – A's 15 % figure comes from an advert and is unverified; B shows keyboard activity is a poor measure of quality. Para 4 – B's warnings about anxiety, 'looking busy' and losing good staff suggest monitoring could reduce real output. Para 5 – own view: use security alerts for sensitive data only, openly explained; manage performance through clear goals and regular meetings; consult staff before any decision. Formal close.
parts.working: Ideas to evaluate: Text A: records programs, websites, keyboard activity, breaks; weekly reports on productivity; 15 % output rise in three months; people waste less time when recorded; alerts if confidential files copied. Text B: activity is not quality (designer thinking vs clerk typing); constant watching causes anxiety and resentment; people fake busyness; good staff leave; set goals, judge results, talk regularly; surveillance replaces leadership poorly. Evaluation points: A is a sales advert with a self-reported statistic; B is expert opinion but offers no figures. Data security is a fair concern that can be met without tracking everyone's activity. Best answers separate the two purposes and suggest a measured approach. Register: formal and polite, persuasive, with a clear purpose in the opening and a courteous close. stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Lessons for life (from a parents' magazine)

Our children can solve quadratic equations and name the parts of a cell, but many leave school unable to cook a meal, read a gas bill or sew on a button. That is a failure of our education system.

Schools should give at least two lessons a week to practical life skills: cooking, budgeting, basic first aid, simple repairs. These are skills every adult needs, whatever career they choose.

Pupils also enjoy practical lessons. Children who struggle in the classroom often shine when they are working with their hands, and their confidence grows.

Text B: Exams come first (a letter to a newspaper from a secondary-school teacher)

The timetable is already full. Every lesson given to cooking or repairs must be taken from mathematics, science or languages, which decide pupils' exam results and their chances of university and good jobs.

Life skills are important, but they are best learned at home, where parents can teach their own family's way of doing things.

Schools also lack the kitchens, equipment and trained teachers that practical subjects need. Rather than adding new lessons, schools could run optional after-school clubs for pupils who are interested.

parts.text:
Your school magazine is running a feature on whether schools should teach practical life skills such as cooking and budgeting. You decide to write an article for the magazine.

Para 3 – Text B's timetable point is the key objection: what would be cut? Exams do shape futures. Para 4 – B's 'learn at home' assumes every home can teach them; A's point about pupils who shine practically matters. Para 5 – own view: build life skills into existing subjects (budgeting in maths, first aid in biology) plus clubs; short course in final year. Lively conclusion to readers.

Text B: timetable full – would cut core subjects; exams decide university and jobs; better learned at home; schools lack kitchens, equipment, trained teachers; after-school clubs instead. Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Pets make a building a home (from a pet charity's website)

Studies show that pet owners are less lonely and less stressed, and that walking a dog is a great way to meet neighbours. Yet many apartment buildings ban pets entirely.

A well-trained cat or small dog causes no more trouble than a noisy family. Responsible owners clean up after their animals and keep them under control.

Banning pets also forces people to give up much-loved animals when they move, and animal shelters are full of pets surrendered for this reason. Buildings should welcome pets, with simple rules for owners.

Text B: Think of the neighbours (from a residents' association newsletter)

Our building has a strict no-pets rule, and most residents want to keep it. In shared buildings, one person's pet becomes everyone's problem.

Dogs barking while their owners are at work disturb residents who work at night or have small children. Some people are allergic to cats or afraid of dogs, and they should not have to meet them in the lift. Corridors and stairs have been dirtied by animals in the past.

Not every owner is responsible, and once a pet is living in a flat it is very hard to remove it, however much trouble it causes.

parts.text:
A community magazine is running a feature on whether pets should be allowed in apartment buildings. You decide to write an article for the magazine.

• evaluate the views given in both texts about allowing pets in apartment buildings
• give your own views, based on what you have read.

parts.answer: Model plan: Engaging headline and opening (a dog in the lift). Para 2 – Text A's health and social benefits are appealing, though from a pet charity. Para 3 – Text B's concerns (noise, allergies, fear, dirt) are real for shared spaces; A's 'no more trouble than a noisy family' is a weak comparison. Para 4 – B admits responsible owners exist; its strongest point is that bad cases are hard to fix. Para 5 – own view: allow pets with clear rules (registration, deposit, lift etiquette, removal after repeated complaints). Conclude addressing both owners and neighbours.

Text A: Pay for results (from a youth charity's newsletter)

Last year our charity offered pupils at two schools a cash reward for every grade they improved by the end of the year. Attendance rose, more homework was handed in and average grades went up.

Adults are paid for doing their jobs well, so why not students? A reward gives pupils, especially those who see no point in school, an immediate reason to try. For families who need their teenagers to earn, the money can also mean a child stays in education instead of leaving to work.

Once pupils discover they can succeed, the habit of working hard stays with them.

Text B: The wrong lesson (from an article by an educational psychologist)

Paying children to learn teaches them that learning is only worth doing for money. Studies of reward schemes suggest that when the payments stop, effort often falls back, sometimes below where it started.

Cash rewards also favour what can be counted. Pupils may choose easier tasks, cram for tests or even cheat, rather than develop real curiosity.

The money would do more good if it paid for tutors, books and study spaces for pupils who need them. Praise, interesting lessons and clear goals motivate young people more lastingly than a payment.

Text A: Name the top ten (from a newspaper column by a former headteacher)

When I was a pupil, the names of the top ten students in every year were read out in assembly and posted on the notice board. It made us work harder than any lecture could.

Every year we hear from pupils who dread the day the rankings go up. For those at the bottom, the list is a public humiliation that can lead to bullying, anxiety and a belief that they are simply 'not clever'.

Pupils and parents should certainly receive detailed results, privately, with advice on how to improve. Progress, not position, is what matters.

Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Goodbye to cash (from a digital payments company)

In many cities, a cup of tea can now be paid for with a phone. It is time to go further and phase out cash altogether.

Digital payments are faster and safer: there is no need to carry large sums that can be stolen, and every transaction is recorded. That record makes it much harder to avoid paying tax or to hide money gained through crime.

Businesses save time counting and banking notes, and customers can track their spending through an app. A cashless economy is a modern economy.

Text B: Cash is for everyone (from a consumer rights organisation)

Millions of people still depend on cash. Many elderly people, people in rural areas without reliable internet and those without bank accounts would be shut out of everyday shopping if cash disappeared.

Digital systems also fail. When networks go down or the power is cut, card machines stop working, and only those with notes in their pockets can buy food.

Cash is private: nobody else knows what you bought. And many people find it easier to budget with notes in an envelope than with an app that makes spending effortless.

Text A: Let the sky light up (from a festival organiser's statement)

Fireworks have marked weddings, festivals and national celebrations for centuries. For many families, the bright colours and loud bangs are what make a special night unforgettable.

The fireworks industry provides work for thousands of people, and public displays bring crowds who spend money in local businesses.

Accidents happen when people use cheap, illegal fireworks. The answer is to sell only tested, licensed products and to encourage large, professionally run displays, not to ban a joyful tradition.

Every festival night, our emergency department treats burns, eye injuries and hearing damage from fireworks, many of them in children.

The smoke from thousands of fireworks makes air pollution far worse for days, which is dangerous for people with asthma and heart conditions. Animals panic at the noise: dogs run into traffic and birds abandon their nests.

There are other ways to celebrate. Several cities have replaced fireworks with light shows using drones or lasers, which are quieter, safer and just as spectacular.

Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Bring back the mammoth (from a science website)

Scientists believe that within a decade they may be able to create animals that closely resemble extinct species, such as the woolly mammoth, by editing the genes of their living relatives.

This 'de-extinction' could undo some of the damage humans have caused. Restored species could help ecosystems recover: large grazing animals, for example, can keep grasslands healthy.

The research also produces knowledge that can help endangered species that still exist, such as techniques for increasing genetic diversity in small populations. Science should not be afraid to dream.

Text B: Save what we still have (from a wildlife conservation charity)

Thousands of species are disappearing right now because their habitats are being destroyed. Every rupee or dollar spent on resurrecting extinct animals is money not spent protecting forests, wetlands and the creatures that live there.

A 'new mammoth' would not truly be a mammoth: it would be an elephant with some changed genes, raised without a herd to learn from, in a world very different from the one its ancestors knew.

There is also a danger that people will stop worrying about extinction if they believe scientists can simply bring animals back.

Para 5 – own view: protect habitats first; allow limited genetic research where it helps endangered species; be wary of complacency. Thoughtful close.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Read Text A and Text B, then answer the question.

Text A: Votes at sixteen (from a youth campaign group)

At sixteen, young people in many countries can work, pay tax and, in some places, marry. Yet they have no say in the decisions that will shape their future, from climate policy to the cost of university.

Teenagers are better informed than ever, and studies from places that have lowered the voting age show that people who vote for the first time while still at school are more likely to keep voting for the rest of their lives.

Politicians would also have to pay attention to young people's concerns, instead of focusing only on older voters.

Text B: Wait until eighteen (from a newspaper editorial)

Most sixteen-year-olds are still at school and living with their parents. Their experience of paying rent, running a household or holding a full-time job is limited, and many say themselves that they do not feel ready to vote.

Young people can also be heavily influenced by teachers, parents or social media, and there is a risk that they would simply repeat the views of those around them.

Eighteen is a clear and widely accepted age of adulthood. Rather than changing it, schools should teach students more about how government works, so that they are ready when the time comes.

Text A: Music for everyone (from a music teacher's proposal to the school)

I propose that every pupil in Years 7 and 8 learns a musical instrument, with lessons in small groups during the school day and instruments lent free of charge.

Learning an instrument builds patience, concentration and memory, and playing in a group teaches pupils to listen to one another. Many children never get the chance because their families cannot afford lessons; a school programme would make it fair.

Text B: Not every child is musical (a comment from a parent at a school meeting)

I am all in favour of music, but making it compulsory is a mistake. Some children simply do not enjoy it, and forcing them to practise will turn music into a punishment.

Where will the time come from? Lessons would have to be taken from other subjects or from break times, which children need.

Instruments are expensive to buy and repair, and the school would need more specialist teachers. It would be better to offer free lessons to every child who wants them, and let the others choose a different activity such as art, sport or coding.

Text A: Home by nine (from a city police proposal)

Over the past year, the number of under-sixteens involved in late-night crime, both as offenders and as victims, has risen sharply. We propose a curfew: young people under sixteen should not be out in public after nine o'clock at night unless accompanied by an adult.

Text A: Assess all year, not in one week (from an education researcher's article)

A final exam measures how well a student performs on one day, under pressure, in a hot hall. Illness, nerves or a family problem can wipe out two years of hard work.

Continuous assessment – projects, practical work and marked assignments spread over the course – gives a fairer picture. It rewards steady effort, reduces panic and tests skills that exams cannot, such as research and teamwork.

Many universities and employers value these skills more than the ability to memorise facts.

Text B: Exams are fair because they are equal (from a newspaper column by a university lecturer)

In an exam, every student answers the same questions in the same time, without help. That is what makes the result trustworthy.

Coursework can be completed at home, where some students have parents, tutors or the internet to help them and others have no one. It is very hard for teachers to be sure the work is the student's own, especially now that artificial intelligence can write essays.

Continuous assessment also means continuous pressure: instead of one stressful month, students face deadlines all year round.

Populations are ageing and there are not enough care workers. Our care robots can remind older people to take their medicine, help them stand up, call for help if they fall and hold simple conversations to keep them company.

Text A: Feedback, not grades (from a headteacher's proposal to parents)

From next year, we propose that pupils up to the age of fourteen will receive written comments on their work instead of marks or grades.

Research shows that when pupils receive a grade and a comment, most look only at the grade and ignore the advice. Without grades, they read the feedback and act on it.

Grades also label children early. A pupil who keeps getting a 'C' comes to believe he is a 'C student' and stops trying. Removing grades in the early years encourages pupils to take risks, learn from mistakes and compete with themselves rather than with each other.

Text B: Parents need to know (a parent's response in the school newsletter)

Comments such as 'good effort, keep working on paragraphing' tell me very little about how my daughter is really doing. A grade is clear, and I can see at a glance whether she needs extra help.

Children are not as fragile as this proposal assumes. Many are motivated by aiming for a higher grade, and they will face grades in public exams at sixteen anyway. Suddenly meeting them for the first time could be a shock.

Writing detailed comments for every piece of work will also take teachers many extra hours. I fear the comments will soon become short and repetitive.

stem: The village school in the hills received twenty solar lamps from a regional charity. Shabana, a pupil of fifteen, was given the job of looking after them. In the first winter, cloud covered the valley for days, the batteries drained quickly and the panels became dusty, so the lamps did not charge properly. Shabana began a chart on the classroom wall to record each lamp's charge and every cleaning. When two lamps stopped working altogether, some parents complained that the school had wasted money, while others offered to help. The teachers then drew up a rota: each week a family took a lamp home and signed a board to confirm that it had been returned in good condition.

parts.text:
You are Shabana, now fifteen. A regional education newsletter interviews you about looking after the solar lamps. Begin your interview with the first question.

Write the words of the interview. The interviewer asks only these three questions:
• How did you come to look after the lamps, and what was the first winter like?
• What did you do when two lamps stopped working, and how did the parents react?
• What would you advise another school that wants to share expensive equipment?

Base your answer on the passage above, but be careful to use your own words. Answer each of the three questions. Write about 250 to 350 words. Up to 15 marks are available for the content of your answer and up to 10 marks for the quality of your writing.

stem: Hamid, a farmer's son from a dry village, wanted a well because the women walked two hours each day for water. The idea came to him after a long drought, and at first many elders doubted that the village could afford it. Hamid collected bricks from a demolished school and used a bicycle wheel as a pulley to lift the earth out of the shaft. The shaft collapsed twice in the wet clay, and villagers worked on ropes in the mud to pull out the men who had been trapped. Hamid and the elders arranged shifts so that digging could continue safely. Since the well opened, forty houses have been connected to a shared tap, and the boys now learn sums in a new evening class.

In her first month she swept the floor, cleaned the ink rollers and sorted paper, and only later was she allowed to set type for the presses.
